Newborn calves are capable of standing and following their dam within hours of parturition, an adaptation to the steep, forested terrain of their Honshu, Shikoku, and Kyushu island habitats. This relatively high neonatal investment is consistent with the pattern observed in other caprines inhabiting unpredictable highland environments, where rapid early mobility is critical for predator avoidance. This solitary birthing strategy, coupled with an extended gestation, limits the annual reproductive output to a single litter per year [F_R_i = single litter per year], placing this species firmly on the slow end of the life-history continuum among ruminants of comparable body size.

The extended association between mother and offspring during this time facilitates the transmission of knowledge regarding seasonal foraging patches and escape terrain within their stable home ranges.

The extended pre-reproductive phase, exceeding three years in duration, is a life-history trait typical of large-bodied, long-lived herbivores facing low extrinsic mortality in stable, resource-limited environments. It stands in sharp contrast to the rapid maturation schedules seen in smaller, more fecund ungulates subject to higher predation pressure.
